Isaac's birth and Sarah's joy (verses 1–8)

Few people in Old Testament times were born with such great hopes resting upon them as Isaac.

In this he was a picture of Christ, the Seed whom the holy God had promised so long before and whom godly people had awaited for so many generations.

Isaac was born according to God's promise, at the very time God had appointed.

Whatever mercy God has promised will certainly come at the time he has chosen—and that time is best.

Isaac means “laughter.”

There was good reason for that name (Genesis 17:17; 18:13).

When the sun of comfort rises over our souls, it is good to remember how welcome the first light of dawn once was.

When Sarah first heard God's promise, she laughed with doubt and distrust.

When God gives us blessings we had almost given up hoping for, we ought to remember with sorrow and shame how we once doubted his power and his promise.

Now God's mercy filled Sarah with joy and wonder.

The blessings God gives his covenant people go far beyond what they or anyone else could have imagined.

Who could have expected him to do so much for those who deserve so little—and indeed deserve his judgment?

Who would have imagined that God would send his Son to die for us, and his Spirit to make us holy, and his angels to care for us?

Who could have imagined the pardon of such great sins, the acceptance of such insignificant service, and the admission of such unworthy creatures into his covenant?

Scripture gives a brief account of Isaac's infancy.

We should recognize God's special care and tenderness in the feeding and nursing of children and in their preservation through the dangers of early childhood (Psalm 22:9–10; Hosea 11:1–2).

Ishmael mocks Isaac (verses 9–13)

This family incident teaches us not to rely on outward privileges or on anything we have done ourselves.

Instead, let us seek the blessings of the new covenant through faith in its divine Guarantor.

Ishmael's mocking was persecution.

He showed wicked contempt for God's covenant and promise and acted with malice toward Isaac.

God notices what children say and do, even while they play.

He will hold them accountable when they do wrong, even if their parents overlook it.

Mockery is a serious sin that greatly offends God.

The children of the promise should therefore expect to be mocked.

Abraham was deeply troubled.

He grieved over Ishmael's misconduct and over Sarah's demand for such a severe punishment.

But God showed Abraham that Isaac must become the ancestor of the promised Seed.

Ishmael was therefore to be sent away, lest he corrupt Isaac's conduct or try to take away his rights.

Abraham's covenant descendants were to be a people set apart, not mixed with those outside the covenant.

Sarah did not understand the full meaning of what she was asking.

Yet God directed her words toward his own wise purpose.

Hagar and Ishmael receive help in the wilderness (verses 14–21)

If Hagar and Ishmael had behaved rightly in Abraham's household, they might have remained there.

But they had misused their privileges and were justly punished.

When we abuse privileges, we lose our claim to them.

People who do not appreciate their blessings while they have them may come to understand their value only when those blessings are taken away.

Hagar and Ishmael soon found themselves in distress in the wilderness.

Scripture does not say that all their supplies had run out, or that Abraham had sent them away without money.

But their water was gone.

They had lost their way, and in the heat Ishmael was quickly overcome with exhaustion and thirst.

Knowing that God is ready to help us in trouble must not make us less active in helping ourselves.

On the contrary, it should encourage us to do everything we can.

God repeated the promise concerning Ishmael to give Hagar a reason to rise and care for him.

We should work diligently for the good of children and young people, remembering that we cannot know what great work God may intend them to accomplish.

The angel showed Hagar where she could find water.

Many people have good reason to be comforted, yet continue mourning because they cannot see that reason.

There is a well of living water close at hand in the covenant of grace.

But they do not notice it until the same God who opened their eyes to see their wound opens them again to see the remedy.

Paran was a wild country, fitting for a wild man like Ishmael.

Those born merely according to the flesh are content with the wilderness of this world.

But the children of the promise long for the heavenly Canaan and cannot finally rest until they reach it.

Yet God was with Ishmael, and his outward prosperity came from that divine care.

Abraham and Abimelech make a covenant (verses 22–34)

Abimelech was convinced that God would keep his promises to Abraham.

It is wise to form good relationships with those whom God has blessed.

We also ought to repay kindness to those who have shown kindness to us.

Wells are scarce and precious in eastern countries.

Abraham made sure his right to the well was acknowledged, so that future quarrels could be avoided.

We cannot demand more of an honest person than a willingness to make things right as soon as a wrong is known.

Abraham now lived among good neighbors, so he remained there for a long time.

He not only practiced his religion privately but professed it openly.

He called upon the Lord as the everlasting God, probably in the grove he had planted as a place of prayer.

He maintained public worship, so that his neighbors could join him.

Godly people should do everything they can to help others become godly too.

Wherever we live as strangers, we must neither neglect nor be ashamed of worshipping the LORD.

Verses 1-8
Few under the Old Testament were brought into the world with such expectations as Isaac. He was in this a type of Christ, that Seed which the holy God so long promised, and holy men so long expected. He was born according to the promise, at the set time of which God had spoken. God's promised mercies will certainly come at the time which He sets, and that is the best time. Isaac means "laughter," and there was good reason for the name, ch. 17:17; 18:13. When the Sun of comfort is risen upon the soul, it is good to remember how welcome the dawning of the day was. When Sarah received the promise, she laughed with distrust and doubt. When God gives us the mercies we began to despair of, we ought to remember with sorrow and shame our sinful distrust of his power and promise, when we were in pursuit of them. This mercy filled Sarah with joy and wonder. God's favours to his covenant people are such as surpass their own and others' thoughts and expectations: who could imagine that he should do so much for those that deserve so little, nay, for those that deserve so ill? Who would have said that God should send his Son to die for us, his Spirit to make us holy, his angels to attend us? Who would have said that such great sins should be pardoned, such mean services accepted, and such worthless worms taken into covenant? A short account of Isaac's infancy is given. God's blessing upon the nursing of children, and the preservation of them through the perils of the infant age, are to be acknowledged as signal instances of the care and tenderness of the Divine providence. See [Ps.22.9] Psa 22:9, [Ps.22.10] 10; [Hos.11.1] Ho 11:1, [2Cor.11.2] 2.
[Gen.21.9-Gen.21.13]
Verses 9-13
Let us not overlook the manner in which this family matter instructs us not to rest in outward privileges, or in our own doings. And let us seek the blessings of the new covenant by faith in its Divine Surety. Ishmael's conduct was persecution, being done in profane contempt of the covenant and promise, and with malice against Isaac. God takes notice of what children say and do in their play; and will reckon with them, if they say or do amiss, though their parents do not. Mocking is a great sin, and very provoking to God. And the children of promise must expect to be mocked. Abraham was grieved that Ishmael should misbehave, and Sarah demand so severe a punishment. But God showed him that Isaac must be the father of the promised Seed; therefore, send Ishmael away, lest he corrupt the manners, or try to take the rights of Isaac. The covenant seed of Abraham must be a people by themselves, not mingled with those who were out of covenant: Sarah little thought of this; but God turned aright what she said.
[Gen.21.14-Gen.21.21]
Verses 14-21
If Hagar and Ishmael had behaved well in Abraham's family, they might have continued there; but they were justly punished. By abusing privileges, we forfeit them. Those who know not when they are well off, will be made to know the worth of mercies by the want of them. They were brought to distress in the wilderness. It is not said that the provisions were spent, or that Abraham sent them away without money. But the water was spent; and having lost their way, in that hot climate Ishmael was soon overcome with fatigue and thirst. God's readiness to help us when we are in trouble, must not slacken, but quicken our endeavours to help ourselves. The promise concerning her son is repeated, as a reason why Hagar should bestir herself to help him. It should engage our care and pains about children and young people, to consider that we know not what great use God has designed them for, and may make of them. The angel directs her to a present supply. Many who have reason to be comforted, go mourning from day to day, because they do not see the reason they have for comfort. Paran was a wild place, fit for a wild man; such as Ishmael. Those who are born after the flesh, take up with the wilderness of this world, while the children of the promise aim at the heavenly Canaan, and cannot be at rest till they are there. Yet God was with the lad; his outward welfare was owing to this.
[Gen.21.22-Gen.21.34]
Verses 22-34
Abimelech felt sure that the promises of God would be fulfilled to Abraham. It is wise to connect ourselves with those who are blessed of God; and we ought to requite kindness to those who have been kind to us. Wells of water are scarce and valuable in eastern countries. Abraham took care to have his title to the well allowed, to prevent disputes in future. No more can be expected from an honest man than that he be ready to do right, as soon as he knows he has done wrong. Abraham, being now in a good neighbourhood, stayed a great while there. There he made, not only a constant practice, but an open profession of his religion. There he called on the name of the Lord, as the everlasting God; probably in the grove he planted, which was his place of prayer. Abraham kept up public worship, in which his neighbours might join. Good men should do all they can to make others so. Wherever we sojourn, we must neither neglect nor be ashamed of the worship of Jehovah.

God tests Abraham (verses 1–2)

We are never beyond the reach of trials.

In Hebrew, the same word can express tempting, testing, or proving.

Every trial tests what is in the heart, showing whether its desires are holy or sinful.

But God tested Abraham without intending to draw him into sin, as Satan does when he tempts.

Strong faith is often tested by great difficulties and called to hard service.

The command to offer Isaac was expressed in words that made the trial more painful.

Every word was like a sword.

First, consider whom he was to offer.

“Take your son”—not your cattle or your sheep. How willingly Abraham would have given them all to save Isaac!

“Your son”—not a servant.

“Your only son”—the only son born to Sarah.

“Isaac”—the very son Abraham loved.

Second, consider where he was to offer him.

The place was a three-day journey away.

Abraham would have time to think about what he was doing and obey deliberately.

Third, consider how he was to offer him.

He was to present Isaac as a burnt offering.

It was not merely a matter of killing his son, his beloved Isaac, but doing so as a sacrifice, with all the solemn ceremonies he normally used when offering a burnt offering.

Abraham obeys in faith (verses 3–10)

Never was gold tested in a hotter fire.

Who other than Abraham would not have argued with God?

A weaker heart would certainly have raised objections.

But Abraham knew the One with whom he had to deal: the Lord himself.

Faith had taught him to obey rather than argue.

He was certain that whatever God commanded was good and that whatever God promised could not fail.

Anyone who consults merely human feelings and reasoning in a matter of obedience to God will never give up their Isaac for him.

The godly patriarch rose early and began his painful journey.

Then he traveled for three whole days with Isaac still in his sight.

Suffering becomes harder when it continues for a long time.

Abraham told his servants, “We will come back to you.”

This shows that he expected Isaac to return with him, even if God had to raise him from the dead.

Then Isaac asked a deeply moving question.

“My father,” he said.

Those words alone must have touched Abraham's heart more deeply than his knife could have pierced Isaac.

Yet Abraham waited for his son's question.

Then, without intending to do so, Abraham spoke a prophecy: “My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.”

Through his words, the Holy Spirit seems to point toward the Lamb of God, whom God would provide to take away the sin of the world.

Abraham arranged the wood as though preparing Isaac's funeral pyre.

Now he had to tell his son the astonishing truth: Isaac himself was the lamb appointed for the sacrifice.

No doubt he comforted Isaac with the same hopes of God's faithfulness that had strengthened his own heart.

Isaac had to be bound.

The great Sacrifice who would come in the fullness of time would also be bound.

When Isaac was bound, Abraham took the knife and reached out to strike the fatal blow.

This act of faith and obedience deserves to be witnessed by God, angels, and humanity.

Sometimes God's providence calls us to part with our own Isaac—whatever we love most.

When that happens, we must submit cheerfully to his holy will (1 Samuel 3:18).

God provides a sacrifice instead of Isaac (verses 11–14)

God had never intended Isaac actually to be sacrificed.

Yet in due time blood more precious than that of animals would be shed for sin: the blood of God's only Son.

Meanwhile, God would not permit human sacrifices to be offered.

Another sacrifice was provided.

We must see here a reference to the promised Messiah, the blessed Seed.

Christ was offered in our place, just as the ram was offered in Isaac's place.

Through Christ's death, our debt was discharged.

Notice also that the temple, where sacrifices were later offered, was built on this same Mount Moriah.

Calvary, where Christ was crucified, was nearby.

Abraham gave the place a new name to encourage believers in every age to trust and obey God with joy.

Jehovah-jireh: “The LORD will provide.”

The name probably alluded to Abraham's earlier words: “God will provide himself a lamb.”

The Lord always keeps his eye on his people in times of trouble and distress, ready to give them help when they need it.

God renews his promise to Abraham (verses 15–19)

In confirming his covenant, God declared his favor toward Abraham more gloriously than ever before.

Those willing to surrender anything for God will find that he makes up their loss with blessings beyond description.

The promise in verse 18 undoubtedly points to the Messiah and the grace of the gospel.

Here we see the loving-kindness of God our Savior toward sinful humanity.

He did not withhold his own Son—his only Son—from us.

And here we see Christ's love: he freely gave himself as the sacrifice for our sins.

Yet he lives!

He calls sinners to come to him and share in the salvation he purchased with his blood.

He calls those he has redeemed to rejoice in him and glorify him.

How can we repay him for all his benefits?

Let his love move us to live not for ourselves, but for the One who died for us and rose again.

Let us admire and worship his grace, giving everything to the service of the Savior who laid down his life for us.

Whatever we love most dearly on earth is our Isaac.

The only way to find true comfort in something earthly is to place it by faith into God's hands.

Yet remember: Abraham was not justified by his willingness to obey.

He was justified through the infinitely greater obedience of Jesus Christ.

Faith received that obedience, rested upon it, and rejoiced in it.

And that same faith prepared Abraham and enabled him to show such extraordinary self-denial and obedience.

Nahor's family (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.20-Gen.22.24" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 20–24</reference>)

The chapter ends with a brief account of Nahor's family, who had settled in Haran.

This genealogy is included because of its connection with God's church.

Both Isaac and Jacob would later take wives from that family, so the list appears before those events are described.

Abraham enjoyed extraordinary privileges, had been brought into God's covenant, and had received the assurance of its promises.

Yet he did not look down upon his relatives.

He was glad to hear that their families were growing and doing well.

It was not in pride that Abraham refused the gift, because he scorned to be beholden to Ephron; but in justice and in prudence. Abraham was able to pay for the field, and therefore would not take advantage of Ephron's generosity. When good parents are neither consulted nor respected, we cannot reasonably expect God's blessing.

Parents, in helping to arrange their children's marriages, should consider carefully what will benefit their souls and help them toward heaven.

Notice Abraham's instructions to his servant. He entrusted the task to someone whose conduct, loyalty, and affection for the household had been proved over many years.

Abraham remembered how wonderfully God's grace had called him away from his homeland.

He therefore trusted God to prosper his efforts without taking his son back to the country God had called him to leave.

What we undertake sincerely for God's glory will eventually bring us comfort.

The servant meets Rebekah (verses 10–28)

Abraham's servant openly acknowledged God.

We are free to bring our particular concerns before divine providence and pray about their details.

The servant asked for a sign.

He did not mean that he would abandon his task unless God gave him exactly the sign he requested. Rather, he was asking God to provide a good wife for his young master.

That was a good prayer.

He wanted a woman who was modest, hardworking, humble, cheerful, helpful, and hospitable.

Whatever fashions may change, both sound judgment and godliness show the value of those qualities in a wife and mother—a companion for her husband, a manager of the household, and someone entrusted with forming the minds of children.

When the servant went to look for a wife for Isaac, he did not go to a place of sinful pleasure or empty amusement and pray to find someone there.

He went to a well, expecting to meet someone properly engaged in ordinary duties.

He asked God to make the right path plain.

The timing of events, no less than the events themselves, is in God's hands.

But we should not tell God too boldly what he must do. If events do not turn out as we demanded, our faith might be weakened rather than strengthened.

God answered his servant and made the way clear.

Rebekah possessed all the qualities the servant was seeking.

She came to the well, filled her jar, and began to return home.

She did not stand staring at the stranger and his camels. She attended to her work and let nothing interrupt it except an opportunity to do good.

She did not begin an immodest or overly familiar conversation. She answered the stranger respectfully.

When the servant realized God had answered his prayer, he gave Rebekah ornaments customary in eastern countries and asked about her family.

Once he discovered that she belonged to Abraham's relatives, he bowed in worship and blessed God.

His words were addressed to the Lord, but Rebekah could hear them and understand something about who he was and where he had come from.

Scripture tells us in unusual detail how Isaac's marriage to Rebekah was arranged.

We should recognize God's providence in the ordinary events of life and practice wisdom and other Christian virtues in the midst of them.

Laban went to invite Abraham's servant into the house—but only after seeing the jewelry on his sister's hands.

We learn about Laban's character from his later actions. It is reasonable to think he might not have been so welcoming if he had not hoped for a generous reward.

The servant remained focused on his task.

Though he had finished a long journey and arrived at a comfortable home, he would not eat until he had explained why he had come.

Doing the work entrusted to us, whether by God or by others, should matter more than our food.

Our Savior said that doing his Father's will was his food and drink (John 4:34).

The servant told them what Abraham had instructed him to do and why.

He described what had happened at the well to support his request, clearly showing how God had guided the matter.

Events that appear to result from our choices, our plans, or chance are appointed by God.

That does not discourage us from using appropriate means. Rather, it encourages their wise and faithful use.

Rebekah's family willingly and gladly accepted the proposal.

A matter that comes from the Lord is likely to bring comfort.

The servant thanked God for the success of his mission.

He was humble, and humble people are not ashamed to acknowledge their position in life, whatever it may be.

Even our ordinary earthly concerns become sweeter when godliness is woven into them.

Abraham's servant preferred his work to his own pleasure and was eager to return home.

A wise and godly person who takes duty seriously has no place for needless delay and idleness.

Children should not marry without their parents' consent.

Likewise, parents should not marry off their children without their own consent.

Rebekah agreed to go and was willing to leave immediately.

Her good character shows that her response was not wrong, even though it did not follow the marriage customs common in Henry's own society.

We may hope she understood something of the faith and godliness of the household she was about to join.

Perhaps that helped make her willing to leave her own people and her father's home.

Her relatives sent her with suitable companions and sincere good wishes.

They blessed Rebekah.

When people we love enter a new stage of life, we should commend them to God's grace and blessing through prayer.

Isaac was engaged in good work when he met Rebekah.

He had gone out in the quiet of the evening, to a solitary place, for meditation and prayer.

Through these holy practices we commune with God and examine our own hearts.

Godly people love times of quiet. It benefits us to be alone often, provided we use the time well.

Indeed, we are never less alone than when we are alone with God.

Notice what a loving son Isaac was.

About three years had passed since his mother died, and only now did he find comfort.

Notice also what a loving husband he became.

Those who are dutiful sons are likely to become loving husbands. People who faithfully honor their first calling in life are likely to do the same in the responsibilities that follow.

Believers' faith is tested and their patience exercised during the waiting.

And blessings long awaited become even sweeter when they arrive.

Esau became a skillful and successful hunter.

He pursued wild animals so effectively that he became a conqueror who ruled over his neighbors.

Jacob was a quiet and straightforward man.

He preferred the genuine pleasures of a private life to outward show and false delights.

In his heart he lived as a stranger and pilgrim, and he remained a shepherd all his days.

Isaac and Rebekah had only these two sons.

One became his father's favorite, the other his mother's.

Godly parents may naturally feel especially drawn toward a child who loves the Lord.

Here we read about the bargain made between Jacob and Esau.

The birthright belonged to Esau by birth, but to Jacob by God's promise.

It concerned spiritual privileges.

Jacob desired the birthright, but he tried to obtain it by dishonest means, inconsistent with his otherwise straightforward character.

He was right to desire the best gifts earnestly.

He was wrong to take advantage of his brother's need.

The question was not who would inherit their father's ordinary possessions. That inheritance was not what Jacob sought in this bargain.

The birthright included the future possession of Canaan by his descendants and the covenant made with Abraham concerning Christ, the promised Seed.

The desire to satisfy bodily appetites has ruined thousands of precious souls.

Those who let their hearts follow what their eyes desire (Job 31:7), or live to serve their stomachs, will eventually suffer for it.

The sisters' desire to become mothers of the promised Seed was good in itself.

But that desire could become excessive and disordered.

They also wanted the honor of many children and feared the shame of childlessness.

It seems clear that both sisters were influenced by God's promises to Abraham.

After fourteen years of service, Jacob was ready to leave with no provision except God's promise.

Yet Laban owed him a fair reward for years of valuable work, and God intended Jacob to receive provision from it.

Rather than agree to fixed wages with a man as selfish as Laban, Jacob entrusted his cause to God.

He appears to have acted honestly, keeping only those animals whose colors had been specified in the agreement.

The desire, good in itself, but often too great and irregular, of being the mother of the promised Seed, with the honour of having many children, and the reproach of being barren, were causes of this unbecoming contest between the sisters. The fourteen years being gone, Jacob was willing to depart without any provision, except God's promise. But he had in many ways a just claim on Laban's substance, and it was the will of God that he should be provided for from it. He referred his cause to God, rather than agree for stated wages with Laban, whose selfishness was very great. And it would appear that he acted honestly, when none but those of the colours fixed upon should be found among his cattle.
